text: As the 19th century drew to a close, humanity seemed to be conquering nature itself. Steam engines drove the factories around the clock. Steel railroads stitched continents together. Thousands of miles of telegraph cable crossed the ocean floor, connecting the world through information for the first time. Science had become a new religion. People truly believed they were no longer at the mercy of nature. They were its masters. The Dutch East Indies, present-day Indonesia, was a vital hub of global trade, exporting coffee, sugar, and spices. Every day, dozens of merchant ships passed through the Sunda Strait, between the islands of Java and Sumatra. In the middle of that strait stood the picturesque volcanic island of Krakatoa. Dense, emerald-green rainforest covered its slopes, alive with birdsong. But Krakatoa sits directly above a subduction zone. Here, the Indo-Australian tectonic plate forces its way beneath the Eurasian plate at roughly two and a half inches a year. Over millions of years, friction and melting rock generate enormous quantities of magma. That thick magma collects in a vast chamber beneath the strait, turning the island into a time bomb, a pressure vessel with its release valve jammed shut. To sailors, it was simply a useful landmark. A beautiful green mountain rising above brilliant blue water. No one imagined that the mountain held enough energy to tear apart the Earth's crust, alter the planet's climate, and show humanity just how little power it really had. 100 years before the eruption. The volcano is quiet. Krakatoa last stirred in 1680, but that eruption was moderate, and the memory quickly faded. Deep beneath the Sunda Strait, tens of miles underground, the Indo-Australian plate continues sliding beneath the Eurasian plate, moving about as fast as a human fingernail grows. A plug of hardened lava has sealed the vent, turning the mountain into a giant, dormant pressure cooker. With every passing decade, the pressure builds. On the surface, it is still a tropical paradise. No one lives on the island, but sailors often stop there to collect fresh water and wood. Beneath the thin crust, andesite and dacite continue to crystallize in the magma chamber. As the magma cools, the pressure from its dissolved gases—water vapor, carbon dioxide, and sulfur dioxide— steadily increases. Deep underground, the spring is winding tighter. One year before the eruption. The telegraph network now spans the globe. News from London reaches Batavia, present-day Jakarta, in a matter of hours. The colonial elite enjoy a comfortable life. Dutch officers and merchants sip gin over ice on their verandas, discussing the latest stock prices. Beneath them, Krakatoa's magma chamber is approaching its limit. Gas pressure inside the molten rock puts the island's rocky foundation under tremendous strain. Around the Sunda Strait, the ground begins to tremble. Local residents notice small earthquakes. But seismology is not yet an exact science. No one knows how to read the warning signs. Nature is already sounding the alarm. No one is listening. Three months before the eruption. May 20th, 1883. The illusion of safety begins to crack. Passing through the Sunda Strait, the captain of the German warship Elizabeth spots a column of smoke and ash rising nearly seven miles above Krakatoa. The volcano has awakened. Deep explosions rumble like distant artillery. In Batavia, people treat the eruption as a spectacular show. Local entrepreneurs organize sightseeing trips to the foot of the smoking mountain. Women in hoop skirts and men in top hats sip champagne on deck, watching the volcano hurl pumice and ash into the sky. They have no idea they are staring down the barrel of a loaded shotgun. And the trigger has already been pulled. Then the activity subsides. Krakatoa seems to pause, lulling everyone into a false sense of security. But it isn't over. Inside the crater, an internal barrier is breaking down. One month before the eruption. The volcano becomes active again. This time, the eruption doesn't stop. A gray haze hangs over the Sunda Strait. Ash blankets the decks of passing ships. Sailors have to sweep it overboard every day. At night, glowing lava bathes Krakatoa's summit in an eerie red light. But the human mind has a remarkable ability to adjust. Even the extraordinary can become routine. Merchant ships keep sailing past the island. Colonial officials keep collecting taxes. No one evacuates the coastal towns just a few dozen miles away. Meanwhile, deep beneath the island, a deadly process is underway. The continuous eruptions are draining the upper part of the magma chamber. Without support from below, the chamber's roof begins to develop tiny cracks. Around the island, seawater presses against the rock, seeking any opening into the inferno beneath it. 24 hours before the eruption. The first explosion. Everything before this was barely a cough. Krakatoa erupts with a violence never seen before. A vast column of black ash punches through the troposphere and rises into the stratosphere, reaching 17 miles into the sky. Day turns to pitch black night. Within roughly 90 miles of the volcano, darkness swallows everything. Only blinding flashes of lightning break through. Billions of ash particles collide and rub against one another in the rising plume, generating enormous electrical charges. Lightning tears across the sky. The British ship Charles Ball is trapped just nine miles from the volcano. Red-hot pumice and pumpkin-sized rocks rain down on its decks. Sulfur fills the air. Breathing becomes almost impossible. The captain orders the hatches sealed. Pounded by waves and falling rock, the crew prepares to die. Deep explosions follow every 10 minutes. Dozens of miles away, the pressure waves strike people in the chest like physical blows. One hour before the eruption. Early that morning, another explosion tears through the island. Krakatoa is already close to destruction. Its structure can no longer hold. The enormous dome of rock above the magma chamber begins to cave in. Millions of tons of seawater rush into the opening, pouring directly onto magma heated to roughly 1,830 degrees Fahrenheit. The physics is simple and merciless. At that temperature, water flashes into steam, expanding to thousands of times its original volume. But the steam has nowhere to go. It is trapped beneath what remains of the island. The pressure rises beyond anything the human mind can grasp. The eruption. The third and most powerful explosion strikes. The energy released in that fraction of a second is estimated at roughly 200 megatons of TNT. That is 10,000 times the power of the atomic bomb that devastated Hiroshima. Four times the power of the Tsar Bomba, the most powerful weapon ever built. Krakatoa ceases to exist. Two-thirds of the island, millions of tons of solid rock, simply vaporizes, becoming searing gas, dust, and fragments of shrapnel hurled as high as 50 miles to the edge of space. But in that instant, the most destructive force is sound. Krakatoa produces the loudest sound in recorded human history. At this intensity, sound becomes a physical weapon. On ships within roughly 37 miles, sailors' eardrums rupture instantly. Many bleed from their ears and noses. The shock wave races outward faster than the speed of sound. In Batavia, a hundred miles away, the blast is so deafening that people rush into the streets, convinced artillery shells are exploding in the next block. Four hours later, the sound reaches Rodriguez Island in the Indian Ocean, nearly 3,000 miles from Krakatoa. If the volcano had erupted in Moscow, people could have heard it in Lisbon. The pressure wave will circle the globe seven times before fading completely. Instruments in London, Paris, and New York will record its passage for five days. Earth's atmosphere is ringing like a bell. One hour after the eruption, an explosion this powerful cannot leave the ocean untouched. The collapse of the magma chamber and the enormous masses of rock plunging into the sea unleash a catastrophic tsunami. A wall of water roughly 130 feet high, as tall as a 12-story building, slams into the coasts of Java and Sumatra. Entire towns are wiped away. The wave does more than flood the streets. It tears away buildings, trees, and soil, stripping the land down to bedrock. In the port town of Anier, a showpiece of the Dutch colonial administration, a massive cast-iron lighthouse is ripped from its foundation and hurled inland. The steamship Biro, anchored off the coast, is swept nearly two miles into the jungle. It will remain there, stranded among the palm trees. People have no chance to escape. More than 36,000 die that day, most of them killed by the tsunami. Across vast areas, falling ash blocks out the sky. Daylight will not return for another three days. 24 hours after the eruption, thanks to the telegraph, the world experiences something new, breaking news on a global scale. Within hours of the catastrophe, newspaper headlines in London, New York, and Boston announce a disaster in the East Indies. The technology that made the Victorian world so proud is now broadcasting the scale of its helplessness. The Sunda Strait is blocked. Millions of tons of pumice float on the surface in a solid layer up to 10 feet thick. For months, ships will struggle in vain to push through the floating rock. One month after the eruption, the effects spread far beyond the Indian Ocean, reaching around the planet. More than 5 cubic miles of ash, along with tens of millions of tons of sulfur dioxide, have been blasted into the stratosphere. High-altitude winds carry fine particles around the globe, and people begin to see things they can scarcely believe. For months, the sky puts on an otherworldly display. Light passing through the stratospheric dust makes the daytime sun appear blue or green. Sunrise and sunset become visions of the apocalypse. The sky burns blood red, crimson, and violet. In New York and London, fire crews repeatedly respond to false alarms. People mistake the glow on the horizon for an enormous fire. One year after the eruption, the sulfur haze in the stratosphere acts like a giant mirror, reflecting some of the sun's energy back into space. A volcanic winter begins. Earth's average temperature drops by about 2.2 degrees Fahrenheit. That may sound small. For the global climate, it is a tremendous shock. Weather patterns go haywire. Record snowfalls hit the northern hemisphere. Relentless rain destroys crops in Europe. Summer is unnaturally cold. Krakatoa becomes a turning point for science. Britain's Royal Society assembles an enormous collection of observations, tracking volcanic ash and unusual skies around the world. The work helps lay the foundation for modern meteorology and the study of atmospheric circulation. For the first time, humanity begins to understand Earth as one interconnected, closed system. A mountain exploding in Asia can bring failed harvests and hunger to Europe. 140 years after the eruption. Today, giant container ships once again cross the Sunda Strait. Passenger jets fly overhead. The age of steam and the telegraph has given way to the internet, artificial intelligence, and Mars rovers. We feel even more powerful than the Victorians did. But sail to the site of that explosion and you won't find empty water. In 1927, a new black peak broke the surface where the old island had been destroyed. The sea began to boil again. The volcano was returning. Local people named it Anak Krakatau, the child of Krakatoa. The magma chamber beneath it never disappeared. The grinding tectonic plates continue to feed it. Anak Krakatau grows at an alarming rate, an average of about 16 feet a year. It is alive, it breathes, and it erupts again and again. In December 2018, the child reminded the world of its parents' legacy. During another eruption, part of Anak Krakatau's flank collapsed into the sea, triggering a local tsunami. The waves hit the shores of the Sunda Strait at night, without warning. The earthquake-based warning systems stayed silent. This tsunami had been triggered by a landslide. More than 400 people died. The eruption of Krakatoa in 1883 is more than a chapter in a geology textbook. It is an enduring reminder that our civilization, with its skyscrapers, satellites, and digital networks, rests on a thin, fragile crust above an ocean of liquid fire. We do not own this planet. We are tenants, allowed to live here for now. And nature can change the terms of the lease at any moment, without notice.
